02 Problem and dataset

Why steam temperature matters, and the data we used

Steam leaving the boiler must stay in a safe and efficient temperature band. Forecasting it one minute early gives operators time to react.

WHERE THE DATA COMES FROMZhejiang, ChinaA coal-fired boiler at a chemical plant, recorded from 27 March to 1 April 2022.

Source: Hu et al., Scientific Data (2025)

86,400

readings, one every 5 seconds

30

variables recorded: 29 sensors plus the outlet steam temperature

530–545 °C

normal range of outlet steam temperature

8.6%

of readings fall outside that range

04 How the boiler works

From burning coal to superheated steam

Animated schematic from the project website. The paper’s process flow diagram is in the PowerPoint version.

1
Furnace

Coal burns with air and produces heat and hot flue gas.

2
Cyclones

Separate solids from the gas and return them to the furnace.

3
Heat recovery pass

Flue gas heats the superheaters, economisers and air preheaters. The superheaters set the outlet steam temperature.

4
Fans

Air fans push combustion air in; the induced draft fan pulls flue gas out to the chimney.

05 Problem setup

Predict the steam temperature 1 minute ahead

Training: first 69,100 rows
Testing: 17,276 rows

The model never sees the test rows while learning.

INPUTS
Sensor readings

Readings from the boiler sensors, including the outlet steam temperature now and 5, 10, 15, 30 and 60 seconds earlier.

TARGET
1 value

Outlet steam temperature 1 minute later.

HORIZON
1 minute

Readings are 5 seconds apart, so the forecast looks 60 seconds ahead.

06 Data cleaning

Missing values filled with autoregression

Primary desuperheating water flow output: original data and filled gap

  • One columnAll readings arrived in a single column.
  • AutoregressionEach missing value is predicted from the values just before it.
  • Number of lagsChosen automatically with the Akaike criterion.
  • Why not simple fillingMean or linear filling can distort the shape of the data.

Five models forecast the temperature 1 minute ahead

Actual and predicted outlet steam temperature, first 600 test rows. The persistence baseline predicts no change, so it lags behind.

Random forest0.20100.27600.9948
XGBoost0.18940.28210.9945
LightGBM0.20670.31190.9933

Errors are in °C on 17,276 test rows. Lower is better, except R-squared.

11 Why linear regression

Linear regression is the best model, so we chose it

MEAN ABSOLUTE ERROR IN °C, LOWER IS BETTER
Persistence baseline
0.5341
Linear regression
0.1393
Random forest
0.2010
XGBoost
0.1894
LightGBM
0.2067
0.1393 °Cmean absolute error
0.1771 °Croot mean squared error
0.9978R-squared
  • Lowest error of the five models.
  • 74% lower error than the persistence baseline (0.5341 to 0.1393 °C).
  • Over one minute the temperature moves smoothly, which suits a linear model.
  • Simple and easy to explain.

12 Reading the results correctly

The website shows only rows the model never saw

80% training: 69,100 rows, used to learn
20% test

Only the 20% test rows (17,276) are shown on the website, so every prediction on screen comes from data that was hidden from the model during training.

WHAT THE WEBSITE SHOWS
20%

Unseen test rows only

The training rows are never displayed. Each predicted-versus-actual comparison is a fair test of the model on new data.

HOW BIG THE ERROR IS
0.03%

Average error

0.1393 °C mean absolute error on a steam temperature of about 535 °C, with R-squared of 0.9978.

WHAT THIS MEANS
No fit problem

Not overfitting, not underfitting

An overfit model would fail on unseen rows, and an underfit model would miss the pattern. With 0.03% error on unseen rows, it does neither.

14 Benefits

What the forecast is good for

1
Early warning

A forecast one minute ahead gives operators time to adjust before the steam leaves the 530–545 °C range.

2
Safer operation

Readings outside the normal range can signal abnormal conditions in high-pressure equipment, so early action lowers risk.

3
Steadier steam supply

Keeping the outlet temperature near its target supports steady steam for the plant.

4
Clear and simple

A linear model is easy to explain and check, and the website shows every input behind each forecast.

Expected benefits of using the forecast in operation; they have not been measured in a plant trial.
